item.title: Snyder Brook
item.description: Snyder Brook runs roughly parallel to Valley Way. Fallsway and Brookbank hug the edges of Synder Brook and feature views of many waterfalls, making either trail a great alternative to the lower section of Valley Way.
item.content:encoded:
Snyder Brook runs roughly parallel to Valley Way. Fallsway and Brookbank hug the edges of Synder Brook and feature views of many waterfalls, making either trail a great alternative to the lower section of Valley Way.

Here's Tama Fall, just off Brookbank.

Upper Salroc Falls.

Gordon Fall.

And these are just the waterfalls with names. There are many unnamed rills and falls along Snyder Brook too.

item.title: Church Pond
item.description: Church Pond is a little more than a mile off the Kancamagus Highway, but it feels much more remote. The usual route to the pond is from Camp Passaconaway via the Church Pond Loop Trail. While this used to be a loop, the east section of the trail is permanently closed, now making it an out-and-back route.
item.content:encoded:
Church Pond is a little more than a mile off the Kancamagus Highway, but it feels much more remote. The usual route to the pond is from Camp Passaconaway via the Church Pond Loop Trail. While this used to be a loop, the east section of the trail is permanently closed, now making it an out-and-back route.

After walking over bog bridges through a beautiful marsh, you arrive at a knoll on the east side of the pond. Follow one of the herd paths down to the shore for some great views especially to the southwest. Here is a dramatic view of Mt. Potash (left) rising on the other side of the Kancamagus Highway. To the right of Mt. Potash is the valley of Sabbaday Brook with the Sleepers in the distance.

Swing to the right just a little and North Tripyramid comes into view.

Although it's definitely past peak foliage, the tamaracks are almost neon yellow this time of year.

Tamaracks are common in New Hampshire, but they almost never dominate the landscape. It's always a pleasant surprise to catch the tamarack show after most hardwoods have dropped their leaves.

item.title: Zealand Notch
item.description: Low clouds hanging over Zealand Notch make for vibrant early fall foliage. Here is a view across Zealand Pond toward Mt. Hale.
item.content:encoded:
Low clouds hanging over Zealand Notch make for vibrant early fall foliage. Here is a view across Zealand Pond toward Mt. Hale.

Another view of the pond further up Zealand Trail.

The colors are especially brilliant around Zealand Falls Hut. This is from the top of Zealand Falls.

item.title: Guinea Pond
item.description: Guinea Pond is located in the Sandwich Range Wilderness, just south of Sandwich Mountain. Black Mountain, a subpeak of Sandwich Mountain, looms over the pond.
item.content:encoded:
Guinea Pond is located in the Sandwich Range Wilderness, just south of Sandwich Mountain. Black Mountain, a subpeak of Sandwich Mountain, looms over the pond.

To the right of Black Mountain is Sandwich Dome, the true summit of Sandwich Mountain.

Zooming out a bit, you can see how truly massive Sandwich Mountain is. From this angle, it looks like an entire mountain range, but geographically speaking, it is a single mountain.

item.title: Mt. Success
item.description: Imagine you are hiking the Appalachian Trail northbound. You are almost finished with New Hampshire. You just have one more climb -- Mt. Success. As you near the summit, you look south to see some of the mountains you have already traveled over, the Carter-Moriah Range and the Northern Presidentials.
item.content:encoded:
Imagine you are hiking the Appalachian Trail northbound. You are almost finished with New Hampshire. You just have one more climb -- Mt. Success. As you near the summit, you look south to see some of the mountains you have already traveled over, the Carter-Moriah Range and the Northern Presidentials.

You push north over bog bridges to the summit of Mt. Success.

From there, you get your first proper look at Goose Eye and the mountains of Maine.

item.title: Monadnock Summit Bog
item.description: There are many tiny microclimates scattered around the summit of Mt. Monadnock. It's fascinating to return to favorite spots at different times of the year. This bog is just below the summit on Pumpelly Trail. Today, the bog is full of spring green foliage.
item.content:encoded:
There are many tiny microclimates scattered around the summit of Mt. Monadnock. It's fascinating to return to favorite spots at different times of the year. This bog is just below the summit on Pumpelly Trail. Today, the bog is full of spring green foliage.

Later this summer, the bog cotton will emerge to dance in the wind (photo from August, 2024).

Autumn brings deep, rusty tones (photo from October, 2023).

And the long winter above 3000 feet is almost entirely black and white (photo from November, 2025).

item.title: Chocorua in the Clouds
item.description: The summit of Mt. Chocorua is often crowded with hikers. Apparently, unsettled weather keeps the crowds at bay. It is a rare treat to have the summit to yourself.
item.content:encoded:
The summit of Mt. Chocorua is often crowded with hikers. Apparently, unsettled weather keeps the crowds at bay. It is a rare treat to have the summit to yourself.

Even though the clouds cover most neighboring peaks, North Tripyramid might make an appearance.

And it is magical walking along the exposed section of Piper Trail.

item.title: North of Lafayette
item.description: The Franconia Ridge is very popular -- especially between Little Haystack and Mt. Lafayette. Day hikers are less inclined to venture north of Mt. Lafayette, but it's just as beautiful. This is Garfield Ridge Trail just north of Lafayette.
item.content:encoded:
The Franconia Ridge is very popular -- especially between Little Haystack and Mt. Lafayette. Day hikers are less inclined to venture north of Mt. Lafayette, but it's just as beautiful. This is Garfield Ridge Trail just north of Lafayette.

Further north, Mt. Garfield comes into view.

And here's a closer look at Garfield with some Labrador Tea blooming in the foreground.

item.title: Alpine Garden
item.description: The Alpine Garden is an area above treeline on Mt. Washington's eastern slope between Tuckerman Ravine and Huntington Ravine. It's a place where several varieties of alpine plants produce flowers in June and into July. June 9 is early for the flowers of some varieties, but Lapland Rosebay (pink) and Diapensia (white) are blooming on the edge of Tuckerman Ravine.
item.content:encoded:
The Alpine Garden is an area above treeline on Mt. Washington's eastern slope between Tuckerman Ravine and Huntington Ravine. It's a place where several varieties of alpine plants produce flowers in June and into July. June 9 is early for the flowers of some varieties, but Lapland Rosebay (pink) and Diapensia (white) are blooming on the edge of Tuckerman Ravine.

The high winds of the Alpine Garden cause the stunted trees to twist into strange shapes or Krummholz.

Despite the difficult conditions, Alpine Azalea is thriving. This plant is in a little nook on the leeward side of a small rock.

And there are large patches of Diapensia and Lapland Rosebay everywhere you look.

item.title: Mountain View Farm
item.description: The Daniel Doan Trail is a little-used route to the summit of Smarts Mountain. The trailhead is close to Mountain View Farm in Quinttown, a section of Orford, New Hampshire.
item.content:encoded:
The Daniel Doan Trail is a little-used route to the summit of Smarts Mountain. The trailhead is close to Mountain View Farm in Quinttown, a section of Orford, New Hampshire.

The fields of Mountain View Farm offer views of the surrounding hills including Mt. Cube.

Smarts Mountain is on the 52 with a View (NH52WAV) list, but most hikers take a different route to the summit. It's a shame. If more people knew about Mountain View Farm, the Daniel Doan Trail might be more popular.

item.title: Mt. Crawford
item.description: It's just over 3100 feet high, but Mt. Crawford has some of the best views in the White Mountains. Crawford Notch is just to the northwest.
item.content:encoded:
It's just over 3100 feet high, but Mt. Crawford has some of the best views in the White Mountains. Crawford Notch is just to the northwest.

Stairs Mountain is further up Davis Path to the northeast.

Mt. Washington is almost due north.

And that's just 90 degrees of the compass. Mt. Crawford has close to 360 degrees of views. It's well worth a visit.

item.title: Monadnock after a Nor'easter
item.description: Yesterday, a late season nor'easter dumped more than two feet of snow on the Monadnock region. The entire summit of Monadnock is under a blanket of white. If you look closely, you can see a lone hiker near the top of the mountain.
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday, a late season nor'easter dumped more than two feet of snow on the Monadnock region. The entire summit of Monadnock is under a blanket of white. If you look closely, you can see a lone hiker near the top of the mountain.

The high winds sculpted dramatic shapes in the snow.

The underlying rock emerges in places to remind us the snow is temporary. Spring is just around the corner. The melting snow will help the alpine plants thrive.
